common_name: Blue Boy Holly (Male Pollinator for Meserve Blue Hollies)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, siting within range of three to five female Blue-series hollies so bees can carry pollen between them.

directions: Blue Boy was released alongside Blue Girl as one of Kathleen Meserve's original Meserve hybrid blue hollies, crossing English holly with the cold-hardy East Asian species Ilex rugosa to bring glossy, spiny, blue-green foliage through winters that damage plain English holly. As a male selection it never sets berries itself, instead supplying the pollen that female Blue-series cultivars such as Blue Girl and Blue Princess need to produce their showy red fruit each fall. Its dense, upright, pyramidal habit works equally well as an unclipped specimen or a sheared formal hedge. Site it centrally among the females it is meant to pollinate, since bees generally only range a limited distance between hollies in bloom.

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring in moist to wet, acidic, humus-rich soil in full sun to partial shade, and site a male plant within range of female plants, since this deciduous holly is dioecious and females need pollination to set fruit.

directions: Japanese winterberry is a deciduous holly native to wet woodlands and streambanks across Japan, dropping its leaves each fall to reveal thick clusters of small red berries on female plants that persist on bare branches well into winter. Its berries and finely toothed leaves are smaller and more numerous than those of the familiar native American winterberry, Ilex verticillata, and breeders have long crossed the two species to combine Japanese winterberry's heavy fruit set with American winterberry's larger berry size, producing popular hybrids such as Sparkleberry and its pollinator partner Apollo. Like all winterberries it tolerates consistently wet soil far better than most hollies, making it a good fit for a rain garden or pond margin. Plant at least one male for every several females, since only pollinated female plants produce the ornamental winter berry display.

planting.note: Plant container plants in spring in moist, acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade, giving the trailing stems room to spread as a low groundcover rather than crowding them against upright companions.

directions: Rugosa holly is a low, mat-forming evergreen species native to cold coastal forests and mountain slopes of Japan, Korea, and Sakhalin, where it spreads as a prostrate groundcover with small, spiny, leathery leaves rather than growing into an upright shrub. Its outstanding winter hardiness made it a key parent in Kathleen Meserve's Meserve hybrid blue hollies, which crossed it with English holly to carry glossy blue-green foliage through winters that would damage English holly alone. It is grown far more often as a breeding ancestor than as a garden plant in its own right, though its low, spreading habit suits a rock garden or cold-climate groundcover planting. Give it the same acidic, well-drained soil other hollies prefer and avoid competing it against taller, fast-spreading neighbors.

common_name: Saluenensis Camellia (Wild Parent of the Williamsii Hybrids)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring in moist, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade, sheltering young plants from harsh wind and hard freezes while they establish.

directions: Saluenensis camellia is a wild species from the mountains of Yunnan Province in southwestern China, first collected by Western plant hunters in the early twentieth century, bearing smaller leaves and smaller single pink to white flowers than the familiar Camellia japonica on an airy, twiggy, fast-growing shrub. In the 1920s, J.C. Williams at Caerhays Castle in Cornwall crossed it with Camellia japonica to create the Camellia x williamsii hybrid group, now prized worldwide for combining free flowering, good cold tolerance, and flowers that drop cleanly from the plant rather than browning and clinging after they fade. The straight species is still sought by camellia collectors for its graceful habit and abundant early bloom. Give it reliable shelter from hard freezes and drying wind, since it is somewhat less cold-hardy than many japonica cultivars.

common_name: Delavay Tree Peony (Wild Maroon-Flowered Species Peony)

planting.note: Plant container or bare-root shrubs in early to mid fall in deep, humus-rich, well-drained soil in full sun to partial afternoon shade, siting it where the permanent woody framework will not need to be disturbed again.

directions: Delavay tree peony is a wild woody species native to open woodland and scrub in Yunnan and Sichuan, China, bearing nodding, cupped, deep maroon to blackish-red flowers held just above finely divided, almost fern-like blue-green foliage. It blooms slightly earlier than the familiar Paeonia suffruticosa garden hybrids and tends to grow as a smaller, more multi-stemmed shrub with a looser, more naturalistic silhouette. Its dark flower color and cut-leaf foliage made it an important parent behind the Lemoine nursery's lutea-hybrid tree peonies in the early twentieth century, and its genes persist in many modern tree peony and Itoh intersectional breeding lines. Avoid disturbing the root zone once it is sited, since like other tree peonies it resents transplanting after it has settled in.

common_name: Yellow Tree Peony (Wild Species, Lutea-Hybrid Ancestor)

planting.note: Plant container or bare-root shrubs in early to mid fall in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial afternoon shade, in a permanent site where the woody framework can remain undisturbed for decades.

directions: Yellow tree peony is a wild species discovered growing at high elevation in the mountains of Yunnan, China, and introduced to Western gardens by early plant collectors in the early 1900s. Its small, nodding, cup-shaped yellow flowers are partly hidden beneath finely cut, dark green foliage, giving a more delicate, woodland look than the large, showy blooms of Paeonia suffruticosa hybrids. The French Lemoine nursery crossed it with double-flowered Paeonia suffruticosa cultivars to found the lutea-hybrid tree peony group, and its yellow pigment later proved essential when Toichi Ito used a lutea-hybrid as the pollen parent of the first Itoh intersectional peonies. Site it in a permanent, undisturbed spot, since tree peonies decline when transplanted after their root systems mature.

common_name: Nakahara Azalea (Prostrate Taiwanese Species, North Tisbury Parent)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring in moist, strongly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade under filtered light, giving the trailing stems open ground to spread and root as they go.

directions: Nakahara azalea is a species native to high mountain slopes of Taiwan, growing as a naturally prostrate, mat-forming shrub whose trailing stems press flat to the ground and root along their length as they spread. It flowers later than most azaleas, opening small red to orange-red blooms in early summer after most spring-flowering rhododendrons have finished. Polly Hill grew it on Martha's Vineyard and used it as the foundation species behind the North Tisbury group of hybrid groundcover azaleas, including cultivars like Joseph Hill and Pink Pancake, passing on its flat habit and late bloom time to hardier garden offspring. Use it to drape over a rock wall, carpet the ground beneath taller shrubs, or anchor a low border planting in partial shade.

common_name: Hiemalis Camellia (Fall-Blooming Species Between Sasanqua and Japonica)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring in moist, acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, mulching well to keep the shallow root system cool and evenly moist.

directions: Hiemalis camellia is a species native to Japan that nurseries and botanists class as intermediate between Camellia sasanqua and Camellia japonica, sharing the sasanqua group's tolerance for direct sun and fast, easy growth along with a wide-spreading, somewhat sprawling habit. It produces an abundant fall-into-early-winter flush of single to semi-double pink or white flowers at a time of year when few other shrubs are blooming. Its genes run through many spreading, fall-flowering garden camellias sold under cultivar names, and breeders at the U.S. National Arboretum crossed it with Camellia oleifera to found the cold-hardy Winter series of hybrids. Give it full sun to light shade and good drainage, and expect a looser, more informal silhouette than an upright Camellia japonica.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in consistently moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade, in a rain garden, bog edge, or border that never fully dries out.

directions: Chrysographes iris is a beardless species native to damp mountain meadows of Yunnan and Sichuan, China, taking its name from the fine, metallic gold veining etched across the falls of its deep reddish-purple to violet-blue flowers. It forms a tidy clump of narrow, grass-like foliage that stays attractive through summer after the late-spring to early-summer bloom passes, and the wild-type species is sold alongside selected dark forms by specialty iris nurseries. Like other Sino-Himalayan beardless irises it wants steady moisture through the growing season and performs poorly if the soil is allowed to dry out for long, making it a better match for a bog garden or pond margin than a conventional border. Divide congested clumps every few years in spring to maintain vigor.
